sections.h2: What should a Wrightsville-area seller know about Johnson County?
sections.html:
Johnson County has Wrightsville as its seat and was created from Washington, Laurens and Emanuel land by a bill dated December 11, 1858. The county's history page describes the setting as rural, with tree-lined streets in town and easy driving to Macon, Savannah, Augusta and Milledgeville. Its 1895 courthouse is on the National Register of Historic Places, so Wrightsville's center has older buildings that an appraiser will see as a separate type of property from farmhouses.

Two smaller places add wrinkles. Kite dates to the 1890s and keeps a museum in a former Masonic lodge. Adrian sits on the line with Emanuel County, and that boundary zigzags through town like a Z, so one street can contain neighbors who file in different counties. A parcel near Adrian should be matched to the right county before you call a tax office.

Census data credits Johnson County with 303.02 square miles of land and roughly 30 people per square mile in 2020. Many listings are therefore acreage, timber or a farmhouse at the end of a county road, and each of those carries its own tax treatment.

sections.h2: How do Johnson County's housing figures look next to its neighbors?
sections.html:
Johnson County's home values sit far below the Census figures for Jones and Lamar counties, and its poverty rate is the highest of the four.

The county shrank by about 800 people from 2010 to 2020 and has regained only a sliver. About one resident in five is 65 or older (20.9%), and 3,217 households were counted for 2020-2024. Sellers tend to be heirs, retirees or owners of a house that has stood vacant. With no permits issued in 2025, there is little new construction to compare against, and buyers look hard at condition and repair cost.

sections.h2: Which Johnson County desks answer which tax question?
sections.html:
Tax work is split between two desks that share the building at 2484 West Elm Street in Wrightsville, ZIP 31096.

  • Tax Commissioner at (478) 864-2565 ext. 1: sends bills, takes payments, supplies payoff numbers and handles tag renewals. Hours run weekdays from 8 a.m. until 4:30 p.m., and the tax commissioner site takes online payments.
  • Tax Assessors at (478) 864-3325 ext. 2: set value, accept returns and exemption forms, and receive appeals. Parcel records are on qPublic.
  • Clerk of Superior Court, 2557 East Elm Street, (478) 864-3484: keeps recorded deeds.
  • Probate Court, (478) 864-3316: opens estates when a deceased owner's name is still on the title.

The county tax commissioner page carries one unusual item. Owners whose timber was damaged and cut after Hurricane Helene can get tax relief by completing the form on the Georgia Forestry Commission's site, adding the supporting papers the form names, and delivering it to the tax commissioner. If you are selling woodland, ask whether such a claim was filed for your parcel.

sections.h2: How does an assessment dispute work in Johnson County?
sections.html:
Georgia taxes Johnson County property at 40% of the fair market value the assessors set for January 1. Owners file a return with the assessors during the first three months of the year whenever the property changed hands or was altered, and a late or missing required return costs a 10% penalty on the unreported value, with interest on top.

A disagreement with the value on your notice starts as a written appeal to the Board of Assessors, mailed no later than 45 days after the notice date according to the state Revenue Department. Name your route in that letter. The department lists the county board that hears equalization cases, a hearing officer and an arbitrator, while Johnson County's own page also names superior court. The assessors can hand you the uniform state form.

If you paid tax that was erroneously or illegally collected, a written refund request has three years from the payment date. When a value drops on appeal, the refund follows without a separate request.

sections.h2: Do Johnson County owners get a local homestead break?
sections.html:
They do not get a local one. The state's county fact sheet records that Johnson County has passed no local homestead exemptions, leaving the statewide exemptions as the only option.

  • You must own the house and live in it as your legal residence.
  • The assessors make the final eligibility call.
  • Applications can be turned in any time, but one received after April 1 takes effect the next tax year.
  • An approved exemption renews on its own until you move, sell or ask for a different type.
  • Personal property returns are due annually by April 1 even if nothing changed.
  • A mobile home needs a location permit within 30 days of being set, and a new permit request each year between January 1 and April 1.

A county can also let voters adopt a freeport exemption for business inventory, requested through the assessors during the same window as returns.

sections.h2: What is the Johnson County payment deadline?
sections.html:
Georgia's built-in date is December 20, and a local authority may choose December 1, November 15 or installments. The county's general information page names no date, so phone the tax commissioner and ask which one governs your parcel.

State rules give taxpayers 60 days after the bill's postmark before interest starts, and later balances may collect penalties. Bills go to the owner of record rather than to a lender, which means an escrow servicer might never see yours. When you move or inherit, send the offices a written change of address.

The Revenue Department's FAQ answers the question sellers ask most. The person who owned the home on January 1 is liable for that year's tax, and Georgia pays no refund to someone who moves out mid-year. Buyers and sellers therefore split the year in the contract.

sections.h2: What if the Johnson County house I want to sell has unpaid tax?
sections.html:
Ask the tax commissioner for a payoff in writing, then ask the Clerk of Superior Court whether a lien appears against the parcel. County liens are recorded in the clerk's office, and the commissioner is authorized to levy and sell property for unpaid tax. The commissioner's tax sales page describes how that works.

At closing, a title company or attorney can disburse the payoff from the seller's proceeds so the lien releases when the deed records. For an inherited house, the probate step has to be sorted out first. A cash buyer who takes the house as-is can absorb repairs and paperwork, yet the payoff, the deed and any estate filing are required in every Johnson County sale.

faqs.q: Which Johnson County office mails my property tax bill?
faqs.a: The tax commissioner, at 2484 West Elm Street in Wrightsville, (478) 864-2565 ext. 1. That office bills for county, school and state taxes. Questions about the value belong with the assessors at (478) 864-3325 ext. 2.

faqs.q: Is there a Johnson County homestead exemption on top of the state one?
faqs.a: No. The Georgia Department of Revenue's county sheet says no local homestead exemptions are offered, so the statewide ones apply. Turn in the application by April 1.

faqs.q: How many days do I get to dispute a Johnson County value?
faqs.a: Forty-five days, counted from the date the assessment notice was mailed. The dispute is written and goes to the Board of Assessors first, with your chosen appeal route stated in it.

faqs.q: What do Census numbers say a Johnson County home is worth?
faqs.a: The Census Bureau's 2020-2024 median for owner-occupied homes is $94,900, with 75.9% of units lived in by their owners. Rent runs about $647 a month.

faqs.q: If I close in January, do I still pay that year's tax?
faqs.a: Yes, the January 1 owner is responsible for the year. Georgia does not refund part-year ownership, so the closing statement normally splits the cost between buyer and seller.
